name: Pulmonary barotrauma
specialty: Diving and hyperbaric medicine / Respiratory medicine

clinicalPearls: Overexpansion and rupture of lung tissue caused by expanding gas that cannot escape, classically during ascent from a dive
Breath-holding during ascent or air trapping from airway disease markedly increases the risk
Consequences include pneumothorax, pneumomediastinum, surgical emphysema and arterial gas embolism
It can also occur with positive-pressure mechanical ventilation at high airway pressures
Presentation ranges from chest pain and breathlessness to catastrophic arterial gas embolism
Management targets the specific complication, with recompression for gas embolism and chest decompression for tension pneumothorax
reference.pathophysiology: Pulmonary barotrauma results from Boyle's law: as ambient pressure falls during ascent, gas in the lungs expands, and if it cannot be exhaled the alveoli overdistend and rupture. Escaping gas tracks into the pleural space (pneumothorax), the mediastinum and soft tissues (pneumomediastinum and surgical emphysema), or into the pulmonary veins to cause arterial gas embolism. Air trapping from breath-holding, bronchospasm or bullous disease localises the overpressure and predisposes to rupture.
additionalInvestigations: Chest imaging for pneumothorax, pneumomediastinum and surgical emphysema
Assessment for arterial gas embolism, which takes management priority
Evaluation of underlying airway disease as a risk factor
redFlags: Neurological symptoms indicating arterial gas embolism
reference.prognosis: Isolated small air leaks often resolve with supportive care, but arterial gas embolism or tension pneumothorax can be life-threatening; prompt treatment of complications determines outcome.
pitfalls: Overlooking arterial gas embolism while focusing on a pneumothorax
Missing air trapping from undiagnosed airway disease as the cause
Delaying chest decompression in tension pneumothorax
Allowing a diver with lung bullae to continue diving
references: Diving and hyperbaric medicine references (standard reference)
management: High-flow, high-concentration oxygen to accelerate resorption of extra-alveolar gas and treat hypoxaemia
Urgent recompression with hyperbaric oxygen for arterial gas embolism, which takes management priority
Needle decompression and intercostal drainage for pneumothorax, urgently when there is tension physiology
Conservative observation for small, stable pneumomediastinum and surgical emphysema
Supportive positioning and haemodynamic support for arterial gas embolism alongside treatment of the precipitating event
On mechanical ventilation, adopt lung-protective low-pressure strategies to prevent and limit barotrauma
Assess diving fitness and treat underlying airway or bullous disease before any return to diving, escalating to critical care and diving medicine specialists for gas embolism or tension pneumothorax
